profile.address: 1725, South Oak Street, Champaign, Champaign County, Illinois, 61820
profile.reading:
The National Petascale Computing Facility, commonly called the NCSA Petascale Computing Facility, is an 88,000 square foot building at 1205 West Clark Street in Urbana, Illinois, on the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign campus, just north of the Thomas M. Siebel Center for Computer Science. It was built on the former site of Illini Field, a campus baseball field, to house the National Center for Supercomputing Applications' largest systems.

The facility earned Gold certification under the U.S. Green Building Council's LEED rating system, reflecting an efficiency focused design. Three on site cooling towers provide natural water side cooling, with the facility run to maintain chilled water around 65 degrees Fahrenheit and room air near 78 degrees Fahrenheit rather than the far colder setpoints common in older data centers, an approach that reduces mechanical chiller use for much of the year in central Illinois's climate. Power distribution runs on 480 volt AC service to cut the conversion losses that come from stepping voltage down repeatedly, and the building draws electricity and chilled water from the university's existing campus utility systems rather than a standalone plant.

On the network side, the facility supports 1, 10, 40, and 100 gigabit Ethernet connections to individual systems, with up to 440 gigabits of aggregate external connectivity, and its network is monitored with deep packet inspection and network flow tracking as part of NCSA's cybersecurity program. A help desk staffs the facility's supported systems seven days a week, 365 days a year, from 7 a.m. to 11:30 p.m.

The building's best known tenant was Blue Waters, the National Science Foundation funded supercomputer awarded to NCSA in 2007 and, at the time of its debut, one of the most powerful sustained performance systems in the world. NCSA has since used the same facility to house newer systems, most notably Delta and DeltaAI, its current generation of research computing platforms built to support GPU accelerated and AI focused workloads for the National Science Foundation's broader research community. The facility's design, purpose built for a machine at the scale of Blue Waters and engineered to be reused efficiently as NCSA's hardware generations turn over, has let it remain the center's flagship computing building for well over a decade, a rare example of a single purpose built structure hosting successive generations of national scale supercomputing infrastructure rather than being replaced alongside each new machine.

reading.body:
The NCSA Petascale Computing Facility in Champaign hosts research supercomputers including Blue Waters and DeltaAI, but publishes no power capacity figure, rack count, or accelerator specifications. Without disclosed capacity metrics, this facility cannot be ranked against commercial AI infrastructure or assessed for its share of grid demand. The absence of published specifications means its role in AI scaling cannot be quantified from operator data.

Illinois has 44 mapped data center facilities, of which only six publish power capacity figures totaling 236 megawatts. This campus ranks seventh in the state by published megawatts, but that ranking reflects only the six facilities that disclose capacity. Most mapped facilities in Illinois publish nothing, making state-level inference unreliable. The campus's actual capacity and position remain unknown.

NCSA Petascale Computing Facility sits on the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign campus and houses NSF-funded research systems. As an academic supercomputing center, it operates under different procurement, operational, and energy cost structures than commercial data centers. Its grid impact and scalability constraints cannot be assessed without published power specifications.
